clinicalPearls: Blastocystis is an anaerobic stramenopile protist and one of the most commonly detected organisms in human stool worldwide, particularly in tropical and resource-limited settings
Its clinical significance is debated, as it is frequently found in asymptomatic people and its detection does not reliably prove it is the cause of symptoms
When symptoms are attributed to it they are non-specific, including abdominal discomfort, bloating, flatulence, intermittent watery diarrhoea and nausea
It is transmitted by the faecal-oral route through contaminated food or water, with the cyst as the resistant transmissible form
The vacuolar form is the most recognisable on microscopy, appearing as a rounded body with a large central vacuole
Diagnosis rests on stool microscopy, though sensitivity is improved by culture or molecular methods, and there are numerous genetically distinct subtypes
Treatment is reserved for symptomatic patients in whom other pathogens have been excluded, with metronidazole or cotrimoxazole commonly used
reference.pathophysiology: Blastocystis is a polymorphic anaerobic protist that colonises the large intestine, existing in vacuolar, granular, amoeboid and cyst forms, the cyst being responsible for faecal-oral transmission. Whether and how it causes disease remains uncertain: proposed mechanisms include degradation of the intestinal mucus barrier, protease activity, alteration of gut permeability and immune activation, and pathogenicity may vary between the many genetic subtypes. Because heavy colonisation is common in healthy people and symptoms overlap with functional bowel disorders, attribution of illness requires exclusion of other causes rather than mere detection of the organism.
additionalDifferentials: Coeliac disease and other malabsorptive disorders
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy with permanent staining for the vacuolar form
Stool culture or molecular PCR with subtyping where available
Testing to exclude other enteric protozoa and bacterial pathogens
Coeliac serology and other investigations for chronic diarrhoea when indicated
Full blood count and inflammatory markers
redFlags: Weight loss, rectal bleeding or nocturnal diarrhoea suggesting an alternative serious diagnosis
Persistent symptoms despite treatment, prompting a search for another cause
Symptomatic infection in an immunocompromised host
Systemic features that would be atypical for uncomplicated colonisation
reference.prognosis: Generally benign; most carriage is asymptomatic and self-limiting, and where symptoms are genuinely attributable they usually respond to antimicrobial therapy, though persistence of symptoms often points to another underlying disorder.
pitfalls: Assuming Blastocystis is the cause of symptoms without excluding other pathogens and functional disorders
Anchoring on a positive stool result and missing a coexisting diagnosis such as coeliac disease or inflammatory bowel disease
Repeated courses of antimicrobials when symptoms are in fact functional
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Exclude other enteric pathogens and functional bowel disorders before attributing symptoms to Blastocystis, since carriage is common and often asymptomatic
Reserve antimicrobial therapy — metronidazole, with co-trimoxazole or nitazoxanide as alternatives — for genuinely symptomatic infection after other causes are excluded
Supportive care with oral rehydration for diarrhoeal symptoms
Reinvestigate for an alternative underlying disorder if symptoms persist despite eradication
Advise food and water hygiene to interrupt faecal-oral transmission of the cyst form
